properties.name: With NO persistent database and the full-text index built in RAM, reflow2's own design loads to fully searchable in 1,098 ms and saves in 1,168 ms — and the dominant remaining cost is build_export_doc on the WRITE side, which nobody has looked at
properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-25 at main `39dbf6d`, immediately after the write-buffer index landed (#330). Release build, **in-memory backend, tantivy `create_in_ram`, no RocksDB, nothing on disk**. reflow2's own design: 3,149 nodes / 13,414 edges / 8.10 MB document.

    LOAD (session start)                        SAVE (session end)
      parse JSON            196.1 ms              build export doc   1,137.3 ms
      open graph             10.0 ms              serialize to JSON     31.0 ms  (7.13 MB)
      import + index        890.6 ms              ---------------------------------
      first search_design     1.4 ms              TOTAL save         1,168.3 ms
      ---------------------------------
      TOTAL to searchable 1,098.1 ms

⭐⭐ THE OBJECTION THAT BLOCKED THIS IDEA IS GONE. When the question was first recorded, hydrate was 8,828 ms and the honest read was "viable for typical designs, a research project for this one". The write-buffer index took import from 8,398 ms to ~890 ms INCLUDING the full-text build, and the whole load is now **1.1 seconds for the biggest, densest design that exists**. Nothing about the storage architecture changed to achieve that — it was a `Vec` being linearly scanned.

⭐ THE FULL-TEXT INDEX IS CHEAP, WHICH NOBODY KNEW. Every earlier figure in this line of work had `fulltext` OFF and was explicitly labelled a lower bound. Measured with it ON, building the entire tantivy index from scratch in RAM costs roughly **190–280 ms** on top of the graph import, and the first `search_design` after it returns 10 hits in **1.4 ms**. The index does NOT have to be persisted to be affordable — it is genuinely derived, and rebuilding it per session is a rounding error against a session's length.

⭐ AND THE DOMINANT COST MOVED TO A PLACE NOBODY HAS LOOKED. `export_graph`'s document build is **1,137 ms**, while serializing the result is 31 ms. So the save side is now 36x more expensive than the JSON encoding it exists to produce, and it is the single largest cost in the whole model — larger than the entire load path. It is the same SHAPE as the import defect just fixed (an internal read pattern, not I/O), and it has never been profiled. **If this model is taken, that is the next measurement, and it is very likely another `Vec` somewhere.**

⇒ WHAT THE ROUND TRIP ACTUALLY COSTS A SESSION: ~1.1 s in, ~1.2 s out, **~2.3 s total**, once, for a design larger than any real tenant would hold. Against a session measured in minutes or hours that is not a performance question any more. It is now purely a DURABILITY question, which is the trade `dec:idea-what-guarantees-the-export-if-the-export-is-the-only-durable-copy` holds.

🛑 STILL UNMEASURED, AND EACH COULD STILL SINK IT:
1. **Accumulated store state.** Confirmation-ledger dates, drift baselines, `write_gen`, the `.id.json` / `.sync.json` sidecars. `fact:export-import-export-is-lossless-but-not-a-fixed-point-until-one-normalising-pass` proved the DESIGN round-trips (3,140/3,140 nodes); it proved nothing about what a running seat believes. This is the way the model fails LATE.
2. **Crash durability.** RAM dies with the process. The trade is bounded loss vs no loss and it is a judgement, not a measurement.
3. **The shared server.** Several sessions share one graph through one process today. In-RAM state does not change that — the process IS the state — but nothing has tested what a server restart means when there is no store to reopen.

📌 BOUNDS: one machine, one design, one run per figure, release build, OS page cache uncontrolled. No sub-sampled curve was taken with fulltext on, so the SHAPE of the index cost against design size is unknown — only this one point.
